intro: One tree, and it is one of only two or three of its kind protected anywhere in Japan. Takakura Jinja no Shibunashigaya grows unsignposted in the grounds of Takakura Shrine in Iga City, Mie Prefecture, a rare seedless-skin variety of Japanese nutmeg-yew whose kernels were once sent to feudal lords. A National Natural Monument since 1932, free to visit, though finding it among the shrine's other trees takes a little looking.
meta_description: Takakura Jinja no Shibunashigaya in Iga: a rare, unsignposted Japanese nutmeg-yew, one of only two or three of its kind protected in Japan.
question_meta: Iga's only mapped tree is Takakura Jinja no Shibunashigaya, a rare Japanese nutmeg-yew, a National Natural Monument since 1932.
question_answer: Iga's mapped tree is Takakura Jinja no Shibunashigaya, a Japanese nutmeg-yew of the rare shibunashi variety, in the grounds of Takakura Shrine. No age has been published for it in any source found; it is documented instead by its rarity, its 3.05-metre girth and its National Natural Monument status since 25 July 1932.
question_context: Shibunashigaya means kaya without the astringency: an ordinary Japanese nutmeg-yew produces seeds wrapped in a bitter skin, and this rare variety's kernels can be eaten straight off the tree. Edo-period locals called them bee-larva kaya and white-rice kaya and sent them to their feudal lords. Only two or three such nationally designated trees exist anywhere in Japan, and a third was struck from the register after it died, which makes this one of the rarer designated trees this site maps. The trunk runs to about 21 metres, forking into two main limbs around two metres up, each splitting again roughly ten metres higher into six branches on the west side, where decay shows, and five on the east. Girth at chest height is 3.05 metres; a smaller figure recorded at the base in the same source is treated as a transcription error rather than a fact about the tree, since a base is normally wider than the chest. Takakura Shrine leaves the tree deliberately unsignposted, a precaution from the era when its valuable seeds attracted attention, so finding it among the shrine's other trees takes patience. Nothing blocks entry to the grounds, and no ticket is needed.

faq.q: What is special about this tree?
faq.a: It is a rare shibunashi variety of Japanese nutmeg-yew, whose kernels lack the bitter skin of an ordinary tree of this species and could be eaten straight off it. Only two or three such nationally designated trees exist in Japan.
Unknown. No source gives an age for this tree, only its designation date of 1932 and its measurements. If you can help date it, tell us.
Yes, the shrine grounds are open and there is no entry charge. The tree itself is deliberately left unsignposted, so allow time to find it among the shrine's other trees.

Take the Iga Railway to Ueno-ichi Station, then a bus toward Toriiide, getting off at the Toriiide stop for a roughly 6-minute walk to the shrine. By car it is about 10 minutes from the regional highway.

trees.story:
The seeds of an ordinary kaya come wrapped in a bitter skin. This tree's do not, which is why it has a name of its own.

Shibunashigaya means kaya without the astringency, a rare variety of Japanese nutmeg-yew whose kernels can be eaten straight off the tree. Edo-period locals called them bee-larva kaya and white-rice kaya, and sent them up to their feudal lords. Only two or three such trees hold national designation anywhere in Japan, and a third was struck from the list after it died. This one has been a National Natural Monument since 25 July 1932.

It runs to about 21 metres. The trunk forks into two main limbs roughly two metres up, and each of those splits again about ten metres higher, into six on the west side, where decay shows, and five on the east. Round the chest it measures 3.05 metres. The same source records a smaller figure at the base, which is physically backwards, so read that one as a slip of transcription rather than a fact about the tree.

There is no sign. Takakura Shrine leaves it unmarked on purpose, because seeds worth presenting to a lord attract people who take them, so allow time to pick it out from the trees around it. Nothing bars the way in.

Nobody has put an age on this one in any source we could find. If you know of a figure, tell us.
